text: As a huge brunch foodie, I really mean it when I say this is definitely one of my absolute FAV brunch places ever. The next day, after a long walk along the Waterfront harbor, we were hungry and in search of another brunch place that would live up to the high bar set by Jeannine's. We literally walked ALL across State Street, but couldn't settle on another place with an appetizing menu that even came close. They were either overpriced for nothing special or just plain basics. Feeling a little defeated, we felt the best bet was to go back to Jeannine's, and it did not disappoint! So needless to say, we were even more satisfied w/ this meal than the day before, and vowed to myself to return here every time I'm back in SB. text: I stopped by for a quick lunch at Bobby's Burger Palace while paying a quick weekend visit to Philly with my girlfriend. All of the burgers are pretty reasonably priced (generally in the range of $6-8 or so), and there's plenty of variety in terms of the kind of burger you can get. I ended up getting the LA Burger, while my girlfriend went for the Bobby Blue Burger. We also ordered a side of sweet potato fries and a milkshake as well. It was pretty packed for a Saturday afternoon; we weren't able to get a seat at the bar, but we ended up scoring a seat at the end of a table. Service was very quick despite the crowd - we got our burgers a little over 5 minutes after sitting down. The milkshake was great - not too heavy, but still tasty as the classic. The fries also surprised me as well...I've had sweet potato fries, and generally I'm put off by the 'sweetness' of the fries. These were more fried and tasted great with one of the many ketchup assortments that were available. As for the burger itself - it was delicious. I have been a hamburger guy my entire life (I detest cheeseburgers), but even with cheddar melted all over the pattie, I still enjoyed the burger immensely. The avocado relish added that unique avocado flavor I'm a fan of, and a mixture of the chipotle ketchup and the burger sauce really brought out the flavor of the entire sandwich. My girlfriend was a huge fan of the Bobby Blue; I thought there was a bit too much Blue Cheese on it, but it was still very delicious as well. So why only 4 stars? Simply put, I honestly feel like I could create this burger if I took a regular pattie and added the accompanying condiments and toppings. Unlike Shake Shack, where you can really taste the flavor in the burger itself without adding ketchup or the Shack Sauce, I thought this was a rather ordinary burger that could be easily replicated. Maybe it's wrong to hold it to a higher standard, but the restaurant is run by a freakin' Iron Chef - I expect to be blown away, even if it's just a burger joint! The meal itself was fantastic, and I'd definitely come back once in a while for a sit-down lunch (it's a bit heavy, so don't plan on doing anything athletic after chowing down). But the real value-add here is the variety of toppings you can add to the burger...just not the burger itself.

text: This restaurant is relatively new to the Alberta Avenue area. It is located on 118ave, at 95th street. Since the first time I ate here, the ambiance has greatly improved (they moved into a space that had been previously occupied by Renato's Italian restaurant, and were renovating the space). The decor is now warm and inviting. They have open seating for larger parties, as well as small tables for smaller groups. Most enjoyably, they have two little sitting nooks that provide privacy and a view of the streetscape. The food is very tasty and well presented. Make sure you're prepared to eat with your hands however, since they don't provide cutlery. You eat your meal by scooping morsels up with injera flat bread, which they refill as required. They have a menu from which you can choose individual items, as well as combination plates. The combination plates feed 2, 4, and I think 6 people. When the food arrives, you'll think you'll have no problem plowing through the meal. Think again! There will be leftovers! Truthfully, you could probably fill three people on the 2-person combo plate! If I remember correctly, a 2-person vegetarian combination plate will set you back about $21. The meat plate for two might run you about $23-25. The menu includes meat dishes (lamb, goat, beef) as well as MANY vegetarian dishes. I have had both and found all of them very flavourful. There are some dishes that are more spicy than others, so if spice is an issue, talk to the server. They will be able to help you chose what is appropriate for your palate. The service is FANTASTIC. The cook has come out every time I have eaten there (5 times since August). She's even given us a little dessert, on the house. The serving staff is friendly, helpful and observant (injera will replaced before you realize you need it). Apparently they hold a coffee ceremony on Saturdays and Sundays around 5pm. I haven't been but I think I will check it out in the near future. I have taken many friends to the restaurant and everyone loves it! I highly recommend trying out this new restaurant. You may want to call to make reservations on Friday and Saturday nights since in it's short existence, it has become a very popular eatery for local residents.

text: I'll start with the good: It's Applebee's, you can tell from the name on the front of the building and from the name on the menus. First you'll notice they have security at night, they have a police officer to watch over the customers. They already have more cameras in the ceiling than your local bank branch. With the police as security, multiple cameras and big "No Firearms" sign on the front door; you would assume it's a rough place, but I have never seen in violence there, but this is not your father's Applebee's. Next you'll notice at night it's more of a sports bar experience (and not a family restaurant). I've heard it nicknamed "Club Applebee's" or another name that I will not say here, but don't get me wrong, this in itself is not a problem. In fact, I went and enjoyed the interesting people and lively conversations. At night, you are more likely to socialize and meet new people. Again, the lively crowd is kinda cool, and I've gone there just for that experience. If there is a football or basketball game on, it can be a fun place to drink a beer. My problem with the place is the service, food and lack of cleanliness. The last three times I've gone there, the gave me menus sticky with food or have dried up food on them, and that's just nasty and disgusting, decaying food contains germs and I don't like having my hands touch old decaying food right before I eat. Also, the silverware they gave me had dried up food on it, each time I had to send my silverware back several times, the last time they gave me 5 sets, and told me to just pick the clean set. I order a draft beer and had lipstick on my glass, so I sent it back and got a glass with dried up wing sauce fingerprints on the outside, the third glass I got was clean, but by that time the bartender made me feel like I was being a pest for wanting a clean glass. Also, the food at night is hit or miss. It might be cold, or the same dish may be half cold and half hot (which is strange). Evening meals there are interesting and lively, but if you want higher quality and service, there's a Applebee's on Lindbergh that's better. If you want a quick good lunch go here. Maybe it's just me but when I go out to eat I don't want to wait for my waiter. After having my 54th Street experience, I don't really see what makes it so popular. text: Several times over the past few months, my husband and I stopped by Wild River Grille and read the menu outside. And every time, we said "Naw, don't think so. Just doesn't seem interesting enough for the money" and went to Silver Peak instead. We wound up at Wild River last night because it was Labor Day, and several of the fancier places we wanted to take out-of-town relatives, such as Sezmu, Johnny's Ristorante Italiano or La Ferme, were closed. So we gave it a try. And our initial reaction about the menu was right. I started with a Raspberry Lemon Drop, which was both too sweet and on the bland side. And I didn't taste or feel the booze at all -- and I almost always do. I ordered a Caesar salad, followed by a smoked salmon appetizer as my main course. The Caesar salad had a few croutons on it, and a bland, uninteresting dressing. The white-bread loaf that came with dinner was extremely blah -- not worth eating. I usually have several pieces of bread, but this time I stopped with one. My salmon was OK -- nice sauce, and apparently they smoke it themselves -- but nothing to write home about. My husband's steak (can't remember what cut) seemed a little tough. My father's pear bruschetta looked just plain odd. If you're going to break the rules with something "traditional" like bruschetta, you have to make sure you break them very well. My dad was probably too polite to say anything about it, but he certainly wasn't raving. When we got to dessert, they had creme brulee on the menu, something my husband and I usually never pass up. But then the waitress said there was a change to the menu and it was now CHOCOLATE creme brulee. Huh? That just doesn't sound right, so we passed. Again, if you're going to break the culinary rules of diner expectation, it has to be spectacular. Two good things: The waitress seemed to know the menu well and gave my stepmother good advice about portion sizes and other choices. And, I really like the decor. All the lights -- candles, strings, regular lighting -- really set a bright, festive atmosphere. But the decor doesn't make up for lackluster food, so we won't be back.

text: I chipped a tooth and needed a crown put in. The dentist I'd been seeing for about 10 years was no longer in my network and would have charged over $1000 out of pocket. When I went for x-rays 2 weeks before the tooth-removal procedure, I was prescribed sedatives because I have gag reflex; I was told to take 4 pills the night before and the rest (about 8) when I got to the dentist for the procedure. I also paid the amount I was quoted right before the procedure and assumed I would owe no more. The next thing I remember after getting in the chair was staggering into my bed several hours later. I thought when my mind was clear that the drugs that knocked me out were excessive and I found out later from my mom, who drove me to and from the dentist, that indeed it was excessive. More on this shortly. When I went back two weeks later to have the crown put in, I was told to pay $64 for sedation that apparently was not covered by insurance. I questioned this because I assumed this was part of my quote, but the staff still insisted I pay. I thought now, whatever. The staff tried to small talk me during ths procedure, but I was not interested in conversation; just put the crown in and send me on my way. Three weeks later, I get another unpleasant surprise; a bill that stated I owe $250 more. There was was no explanation. I had to call back the next day and a lady said it was for additional sedation to put me to sleep. I assumed this was covered either by insurance or the quote. I was not told of this beforehand and I was very upset about that, with good reason. The lady said the quote was no guarantee of actual charges insurance would pay. I was lied to and told the woman that on the phone. The woman told me not to yell and scream Lady, I will calm down when you tell me the truth. I later found out from my mom they gave me additional drugs without consent from me (because I obviously was in no condition to consent and if I was I would not have consented) or from my mom (she said the staff did not ask her).. I find this cowardly and unprofessional. Also if there were complications - it's very possible - that is grounds for malpractice. I had to pry from the lady on the telephone I was being charged for this excessive sedation as well as labor for doctor; isn't this what the dentist is being paid for? I will pay this only because I do not want to deal with a collection agency and, though I have a good case, don't want to pay attorney fees that would be more than my bill. So far, the amount I've had to pay out of pocket is what I would have with my previous dentist, who was up front and did not sneak any bills by after the fact. text: Ok, so strictly speaking I ended up not getting my car serviced here (although I did for my last major check up). The first few dealerships were all close to each other in the mid 300s range. However, I started getting a few dealerships that were in the mid 200s range. I started doubting my fading hearing abilities and decided to call back to Del, which was in the 300 range. Surely when I did this years ago and they were the cheapest; things could not have changed that much, right? I got a different person who quoted me a completely different price. The first lady was very nice and quoted me a price of $369 and was nice enough to tell me they would give me a loaner car and there was a 10% discount special running (she may have been mistaken, because looking at their website it was a $20 off coupon, however I know instead of the $20 they used to run the 10%, so...). However, the man I spoke to on the 2nd call quoted me a price of "4 and a quarter" (I am assuming $425) and said it may be even higher than that depending on the exact type of coolant that was in my vehicle. What the heck? Don't they have charts for the amount charged based on make and model? Needless to say I am now very suspicious and probably won't be bringing my car back here. text: 2.5 stars. I really wanted to like this place, but damnit, they failed. Not awful but not worthy of the current 4.5 star rating. And the food was meh for being a New Orleans southern restaurant. Here's what we had: App: crawfish etoufee - very tasty, no complaints about this except the price ($7 for a little cup!) Soup: Gumbo - this was okay but they got the gumbo's mixed up and gave me the chicken one instead of the seafood one Main: bf had "A Taste of Soul" Platter - Filé Gumbo, Red Beans & Rice, Jambalaya, Greens, Fried Chicken, Catfish Strips, and Bread Pudding, collard greens, while I had: Stuffed Bell Pepper - A green bell pepper stuffed with ground beef, shrimp, spices, and seasonings, baked and topped with our light home-style brown gravy, with red beans/rice, and mac/cheese shared the bread pudding for dessert BF really enjoyed his entree, while I found everything about mine to be lacking. BF's was good because all the fried seafood was low in fattiness, had a nice cornmeal crust and was light on oil. Mine sucked because the stuffing in the bell pepper was just whatever, and the mac and cheese was embarrassing - it had the texture of being reheated leftovers (overly mushy noodles and hard cheese) and tasted like almost nothing, box kraft is better. And it was not hot like the bell pepper. The cornbread was not warm either so I didn't get to enjoy any nice crust on top. Bread pudding dessert was hot and delicious, though it had nuts so it automatically became all mine. This was the best part of the meal. Beyond the food being less than impressive, at least my dish, the service was pretty lacking. It took a looong time for a server to get to us, while a neighboring party sat down later, ordered and received their food before us. Another neighboring party had super crappy service too, and even asked for a comment card, and of course did not get one. They could have walked out and not paid, given that they had to actually flag someone else down and ask them to please take their money so they could go, those words literally. So, I say there is a lot of room for improvement here.

text: We had a tower room for $150. This hotel offers pretty poor value for that price. If you can get a room for $50, then you're welcome to add a star. The TV was a tiny tube model with a poor picture--NBC was unwatchable. The remote control had no batteries (quickly remedied by maintenance), but one would think that housekeeping would have discovered the flaw. In addition, the clock was flashing the wrong time, another thing one would think housekeeping would fix. A call to housekeeping for an extra set of towels was promptly answered. However, the washcloths were threadbare. The towels were absorbent, if small. Pillows are cheap and thin and extras weren't provided in the room. Decor was unremarkable, but our view of Reno was nice. The pool is okay. We chose this place because they keep the pool open until 10 pm; most casinos close it way too early to force customers into the casinos. Unfortunately, the construction of the new tower means that there are only two relatively small and plain pools, one for kiddies and slightly deeper one. Valet parking was efficient and courteous, but we checked in and out when crowds were low. I'd have rated this place with three stars except that the price was high, and they tried to tack on a nearly $4 "energy surcharge" at check-out, a despicable practice that more and more hotels try to sneak past their customers. The desk clerk removed it when I protested. ("You didn't see the notice on the PIN pad when you checked in?") READ YOUR STATEMENTS, FOLKS! Avoid the automated checkout if you don't want to get ripped off! We ate at the Buffet. The food is average buffet fare, but the price is pretty reasonable, especially if you use a coupon. text: One of my favorite coffeshops in New Orleans! I definitely took advantage of their late operating hours a few years ago when insomnia and I were BFFs. There's a bookshelf in the middle room with a whole lot of random books for your perusal and the wifi (though sometime shaky) is free. Not to mention a shelf with all sorts of old games (Cold War-era Trivial Pursuit, anyone?) to keep you occupied if you happen to find yourself there without a book or a laptop or something to pass the time. They sell organic and fair trade coffee, if that's your sort of thing. I'm not a coffee drinker but they do have a somewhat exhaustive tea selection (the list is long enough to be kept in a binder at the front counter) and the baristas are more than happy to recommend flavors to you if you're not sure what to get. Their hot cocoa is excellent, too. There's always an assortment of pastries available and a good number of those are vegan and delicious. Don't expect frappucinos or fancyschmancy expensive drinks from Zotz. They're cheap, simple, honest, and good. Oh yea, and there's a free condom bowl. They're responsible, too.

Service - perfectly pleasant. The woman who waited on us knew the menu, served the food promptly and quickly opened the BYOB bottle of wine we had brought with us. text: Again, people argue back and forth as to where you can get the best Mexican food in Tucson. It's kinda like arguing about which politician is most corrupt in Washington; Tucson is frankly a Mexican food mecca. Now, each restaurant has a distinct feel, distinct styles, and I often change which restaurant I take my visitors and friends to based on their individual tastes and wants. After all, if you're going to visit Tucson you want to have a good meal. La Poca Cosa comes to mind, or Mi Niditos, but my goto for showing non-Tucsonans how varied and diverse Mexican style food can be is Guadalajara Grill. Of course there is the standard Mexican food fair--burritos, tacos, enchiladas, but what makes Guadalajara unique is the diversity dishes. You can order anything from a molcajete bubbling with peppers and carne asada to the standard Tres Amigos, all with fresh in-house-made tortillas and at-the-table made salsa. Because my family and friends trek from the Midwest, they are often floored by how varied Mexican food can be from what they know, especially the seafood dishes which are pretty fantastic. Seafood in the desert? Yeah, the Baja is only 3-4 hours away. If you want more than just a meal, Guadalajara sports a meandering mariachi band, and they will come to your table to ask if you'd like a song. Many amors and corazons later, your date or family will be laughing and having a good time. If you want some margarita, they are strong and cheap on certain days so swing by, only complaint there is a little salty (but I like salty margaritas). I highly recommend Guadalajara.

text: Cleanliness: I've ridden train/bus systems in San Fran, Chicago, D.C. and NYC. Philly trains are generally(though not always) far more dirty than either San Fran or D.C. trains. Depending on the stop you get on/off of here in Philly you may encounter the smell of urine which is also part of my "fond" memories of Chicago mass transit. Somehow the City Hall station always smells of something and is really dirty. The Metro lines at DC are the cream of the train lines that I've ridden on. Clean trains, very clean stations, and friendly workers. Reliability: As far as SEPTA reliability, I"ve had fairly good luck with the Orange/Broad St. Line. However when I've switched over to go to West Philly, then the trouble starts. The trains that I've taken to West Philly may or may not be on time and may or may not have room. Not to mention there isn't enough seating for the masses that accumulate when the trains aren't on time. Service: Hands down, SEPTA workers have to be the surliest, most customer unfriendly of all the mass transit workers I've encountered. I've worked in service industry positions before so I know how people can be idiots, but still, there is a level of uncaring and downright hostility that exudes from the majority of the ticket takers I've encountered here. So far for me its been a mixed bag. I get to where I want to go, but I do feel like I need to take a shower after riding on some of the train lines. text: I've stopped in on a couple occasions to catch up with some friends who were randomly visiting from out of town. During those times I was either in for a quick visit, or a fast bite to eat, and I managed to have a good time. But now I think I'll keep it that way (if I ever show up again) because drinking there was downright awful! If a bar side patron has an empty glass in front of him and is looking toward your direction, then it should be a good indicator that he's either ready to get another drink or settle out. It should especially be a good indicator when there's only ten people at the bar and that patron is the only person trying to get your attention. And it should be a super huge "SERVE US ALREADY!" indicator when by the time 5+ minutes goes by another one of that patron's friends has his drink downed and the empty glass in front of him, his other friend has his drink nearly downed, and they're all trying to call your attention without sounding like assholes! I'm sure you know where this is going by reading that last paragraph, But let's just say that calling our bartender for the evening un-attentive would be an understatement! when she wasn't walking by us to talk to some regulars at the other end, she was leaving the bar completely unattended in order to help an off duty worker set up decorations which is something that could be done during a time that most bars don't consider prime business hours. during those moments that she finally came to check on us my mind was racing with thoughts straight out of this talk thread - http://www.yelp.com/topic/mount-laurel-lost-in-translation. It kind of sucks that their service was downright useless because the bar had it's potential. That fact that I know friends who consider themselves to be somewhat regulars means that this place has to have their good days (a lot of my friends are wrong in their decisions but I normally trust that bunch on their choices.). The menu looked promising, and they had more bottles behind the counter than I've seen at any other bar I've ever been to (they even had mead and ginger brandy!). So if they got their act together they could be a solid suburban bar. Until then or always I'll just be at spots like McShea's and Erin Pub when I'm doing the suburbia lifestyle.

text: Was in Tucson for one night this past week for the ACDA convention and this was the hotel we were all booked at. I'm giving it 2 stars mainly because it was clean (for the most part), we didn't see any cockroaches and the staff were pleasant enough. But the actual quality of the room I would rate 1 star. This hotel was $140/night but I honestly think the Motel 6 down the road for $40/night would've been the same quality. The hotel was likely made in the 50's or 60's and they've not renovated it since. I would honestly believe that the mattresses and the pillows have been around as long as well! The room itself was fine but since the beds and pillows were so uncomfortable, I didn't sleep more than 2-3 hours combined over the night. It didn't help that the air conditioner rattled like you wouldn't believe! The next morning after my horrible night of sleep I showered in the strangest bathroom ever. Who puts dropped ceilings in a bathroom? If you were over 6 feet you would've been crouching. And to top it off, the shower didn't drain properly so it was more like a shower/bath...not really pleasant. Also to note there is absolutely nothing to do down in this area of Tucson. The nearest drug store is over 2 miles away and the restaurant selection is poor (although the Caffe Milano nearby was good). Who knows where the nearest Starbucks is...and don't trust the sign that says, "We brew Starbucks Coffee at our Coffee Shop". Their "coffee shop" is their "gift shop" and while Starbucks isn't the greatest coffee, this was definitely worse than Starbucks...maybe they bought it 5 years ago and it's been sitting around all this time. That being said, I don't want to totally hate on this place. As I mentioned, the rooms were relatively clean, staff was friendly and while they don't have a gym, you can get a pass to go to the local YMCA (which is about 4 long blocks away). But honestly, if I were ever to go back to Tucson (which is not something that I hope will happen) I wouldn't go back to this hotel even if you paid me.

text: I was in town for a family visit from Los Angeles. I grew up less than a miles from Forest Park, and had always wanted to visit this restaurant, since it's setting was historical. We were told 60-90 minutes, and had informed them that we were going to take a paddle boat, but would be leaving someone to inform us if a table became available. So, we asked how long would it be to get another table, and were informed bruskly: "well, you're at the bottom of the list now". The person we had left at the desk had not moved from their post, and did NOT hear any call of our name or party number. I can only assume that the hostess didn't see our large numbered party and assumed we had left. We asked the manager. The manager informed us "well, it's your fault, you went out on a boat". (yes, it was, but the rudeness was uncalled for, and we were assured that our wait would be well over an hour). Large parties are hard to seat, but for them to be as rude as they were was uncalled for. We left after 2 1/2 hours with hungry kids and upset adults. Inconsiderate staff and rude manager. Sadly, people will always go, because of the boats. If you want to eat, don't plan on taking a boat ride!

text: Beware of East Coast Super Subs. The moment your eyes touch down on the menu, a challenge is issued: 8" or 16"? What are you, some sort of sissy? Are you really going to be satisfied with just 8 inches of sandwich? C'mon, get the 16". You can handle it! If 16 inches of sandwich -- and not just sandwich, but meaty, cheesy, happiness-filled sandwich -- strikes you as completely ridiculous, then you're probably safe. But if you're an idiot / garbage disposal like me, it sounds just crazy enough to work. So 16 inches of Broad Street Bully it was: an overstuffed monstrosity of Philly steak, provolone, lettuce, tomato, fried onions, and hot peppers, the sort of thing you know you should eat alone so that no one will see the carnage unfolding between your hands and your throat. They handed me the bag containing what looked like two separate sandwiches -- only I knew that it was actually just one enormous awesome sandwich in disguise! Let me start by saying that this sandwich is utterly delicious. It's been said before, but the hot peppers totally make it. Well, the hot peppers and the fried onions. And the steak and cheese and...well okay, the point is: the ingredients here are all really good, and they work together fabulously. The difference in quality between one of these sandwiches and a Frankie's cheese steak is night and day (though Frankie's gets props for sticking with tradition and supplying me with Cheez Whiz). In fact, it was so good that I was finished with the first 8-inch half of the sandwich before I stopped to think about what was happening. My main thought was, "Oh man that was amazing. Thank god there's more." And then, nom nom nom nom... I ate the whole thing. I probably shouldn't have; I couldn't move for the rest of the day. But oh my gosh was it tasty. I would definitely recommend checking this place out. Just do yourself a favor: get the 8".

text: Oh. It's You, New Century Travel. One question haunts me as I contemplate ever riding you again: Was it good for me? Sure, you're a cheap ride that conveniently satiates my desire for round trip tickets on your cushy self, sitting next to the mysterious stranger who becomes my new best friend for about 2 hours--or 5 hours last year when we were broken down on the highway in 95 degree weather, waiting for another bus to bring us more gas when you had a leak -- but there are other fish in the sea that I've been hearing about, and there is nothing positive that distinguishes you from them. There is no reason to go here, ever, unless you are in Blue Bell (god help you), and its late, and you are hungry. I wanted to tell the server so she could get it fixed but she didn't come back or near us for almost 30 minutes, so I just ate half of it. She didn't offer to comp the meal (which I think is what should have happened) nor did she even offer to give me my beer for free (a cheaper and also acceptable alternative). Another time when my friend's band The Saddle Tramps were playing there we all went and tried the special "Trailer Ale" beer they had brewed for the occasion. When the waitress brought me the beer it looked a lot lighter than the (already light) one I had tried but I know that different batches or even the end of a keg can produce different looking and tasting beer so I thought nothing of it until I drank the beer. It tasted NOTHING like the original beer I tasted on my first sit down. Finally when the server came back (it was really busy) I told her and instead of asking the bartender, or having an explanation she just offered to replace it with something else. I find it unacceptable to be a brewery but have no excuse for serving soda water and some other beer. I think they ran out of the beer they called Trailer Ale and thought nobody would notice when they watered down another beer. text: I feel like I'm supposed to like this place. I mean, all the cool kids do, right? Lucky for you (and me?) that I'm not cool. The ingredients for a successful, awesome diner seemingly are there. Kitschy decor? Check! Buddy Holly glasses-wearing servers? Check! Chrome galore? Check! A variety of food and drink for late night? Check! Sadly, these things don't add up to fabulous like they ought. First, it never, ever makes sense to have smoking and non-smoking sections at a small restaurant -- ESPECIALLY WHEN THERE'S NO SEPARATION BETWEEN THE TWO. Seriously, why do restaurants continue to think this is a good idea? This, alone, would be my reason not to come back, if there weren't other things wrong. And there are. Like others have said, City Diner is understaffed. I've only gone to the diner post-8 p.m., so maybe this is only a dinner and late-night thing, but it's still not cool to wait in a near-empty diner for 15 minutes just for a drink order, and then another 20 minutes to have food orders taken. And the food... just... meh. I know it's diner food and isn't meant to be compared with a $100 meal elsewhere, but the food really isn't that great. My usual has been a milkshake and hashbrowns. While the milkshake was indeed thick and tasty, the hashbrowns are way more oily than even at Denny's. It's the same with the other food. Salad should be easy, but there are too many brown pieces of lettuce. Pancakes should be good, but they're too heavy and oddly oily. It's a pattern. And finally, the servers. They're too cool for school. The "you'll wait 15 minutes while I finish my smoke and chat with the cook" thing happens so much that you'll find yourself wanting to say "Screw it!" and leave. Believe me, I've done it. Positives: As mentioned, the milkshakes are good. The decor is fun and interesting. I'd love to hang around and peek at every single thing on the walls. I won't, though, because I won't be back, thanks to the other things I've listed. Bummer.

text: Just went here recently with some friends from my church---first time in a long time and I was pleasantly surprised. Not much has changed in way of food (except this time, I thought the chicken tikka masala was weird---maybe their sauce didn't have as much cream as I'm used to but Karma, over on Chestnut, btw. 2nd and Front, blows New Delhi's out of the water---and yes, I know, chicken tikka masala is not really authentic Indian food. Whatever. It's still pretty delicious.) Anyway, food was great this time around and wish I had went back one more time to the buffet. Typical offerings---samosas, naan, vegetable and chicken curries, rice, papri chaat, salad. I chose kulfi ice cream for my dessert (comes with the buffet price) and I love love love kulfi---this was delicious--I like the whole cardamom taste of it. A bit icy but nothing I couldn't overlook. Also had masala chai with it (well, not really chai---masala tea which I then added my own cream to) and it didn't disappoint. By the way, the masala tea is included in the buffet price, which I didn't know before...wish I did...would've ordered it every time I went in college. The pleasant surprise came from the decor. I haven't been here in a couple of years. In college, we used to joke that when eating at New Delhi, you always needed to adjust your eyesight because the lights got progressively dimmer throughout the meal---so much so that you practically couldn't see what you were eating by the end. Maybe some thought it was for the ambiance but we all thought it was because they were trying to hide a dirty carpet. Well, the "dirty" carpet is no more---the restaurant is much bigger, cleaner and more polished than before. It's lost that typical, mom and pop-Indian restaurant feel, with a fancy-looking bar and bright lighting. When I first walked in, I almost turned around because I thought I accidentally walked into one of the adjacent restaurants. Definitely recommend it. Come here if you're in the area.

text: Peter Chinn's, in what was recently Cheeseburger Charley's, was a surprising delight. The sparse surroundings are a stark contrast to the warm inviting open arms of the corn wrapped goodness these digs churn out. Seating is a little awkward, but who cares, you are there for the food, right? Right. So I'll talk about the food. In the few times I've consumed at this eatery I haven't gotten past the kogi, spicy pork, and bulgogi tacos. If you are scared of spice or a noob, I'd start with the bulgogi. The beef in the bulgogi was fresh, tender, and cooked to my liking (medium rare to medium). I found it to be a little more bland than I prefer, but i'm a spicy food guy. I was not at all turned off by it, but less interested than my other two meaty endeavors. 2nd in line is the kogi. Being unfamiliar with kogi in general i didn't know what to expect. The cilantro lime flavor, fresh cucumber, and other unidentifiable Korean flavors play a cool and savory note. The pork was tender and reasonably seasoned. My personal favorite so far is the spicy pork. An almost fruity but hot barbecue sauce sets this morsel off. Hot enough to make your nose run, but not enough to make the bathroom unpleasant. The sweet and spice of the sauce are intertwined nicely, and don't overpower each other. Don't get me wrong, you may not have a religious experience during your first trip. I can't say the food is mindblowing or has changed my life, but for some reason I keep wanting to go back again and again. I couldn't give it a 5 star rating, simply because the atmosphere is almost food factoryesque and uninviting. That being said, I think our political leaders should look to food for diplomatic inspiration. We should start dropping tortillas on North Korea any time they act up. This might be the solution to the very angry and ronery Kim.Jong- Il. If only Hans Brix would have stumbled upon the taco trucks of California then maybe the DPRK could take a lesson from LA. At least with the food. The marriage of Mexico, Korea, and Los Angeles does indeed make a happy reception in my mouth. (btw don't tell anyone that South Korea has access to these, or WWIII might break out) Oh, and try the onion rings. EDIT: I miss this place. Wish it would reopen.

text: Hailey's is a true "salvage" place. There are many other places in Nashville with salvage in the name, but it's not real salvage or any cheaper than anywhere else. At Hailey's you can find building materials that have obviously been salvaged from demolitions and renovations. This would be the perfect place to go if you're renovating an older home and you want to replace or re-introduce vintage fixtures. They have everything from sinks to light fixtures to storm doors and many other nick nacks. The most incredible things available are clawfoot tubs, of which there are rows outside, vintage sinks, and ornate mantlepieces and iron fireplaces surrounds. I saw one gorgeous wooden mantlepiece in perfectly good condition that could be stripped and mounted with very little trouble and expense. Hailey's doesn't have prices on anything, but it works this way: look around, find something you like, and then ask how much they want for it. I would make this a first stop if you're renovating before you buy an expensive reproduction.

text: Beer World is a textbook example of not judging a book by its cover. Behind the somewhat ghetto exterior of a converted Circle K convenience store lies a mecca of beer goodness. Ignore the exterior windows filled with neon signs for the big commercial brewers like Budweiser, Miller, and Coors. You aren't at your local 7/11. Instead make it to the back two rows of the store plus along the refrigerator wall and savor a world of Belgian, German, British, Polish, and domestic craft beers. All the big names can be found here and every square inch of the place is loaded with boxes and racks of beer. A small selection of what they have to offer includes the following domestic micros: Bell's, Brooklyn, Cigar City, Coney Island, Dunedin, Dogfish, Harpoon, Magic Hat, Ommegang, Rogue, and Terrapin. And outstanding Belgians like: Affligem, Chimay, Delirium, Duvel, Gulden Draak, St. Bernardus, and Saxo. Most selections are available in room temperature 4, 6, and 12 packs. But you can also mix and match among the refrigerated back wall and there are coolers of some of the more popular champagne style 750ml bottle conditioned beers too. The prices are probably slightly above average. It's definitely not as cheap as Total Wine, but with that being said - it's a local business and I don't mind spending a dollar or two more to support a small mom and pop place. The only other thing to keep in mind is to check date on your bottles because they do tend to carry a lot of older stock. With a selection as wide and varied as Beer World's this can be expected since there probably isn't an audience for everything they carry. Overall, a pretty amazing store and worth a trip to poke around for 30 minutes and see what they happen to have in stock. So if you are in the Largo area, I would recommend that you stop in.

text: Once upon a time, there was a venerable, well-established (1928) restaurant in Santa Barbara named Casa de Sevilla, which eventually closed its doors. The name lives on in a new (2005) restaurant in the same location called, simply, Sevilla. Contrary to the name, however, the food has nothing whatsoever to do with Spain, or even Spanish-influenced cuisine. According to the website, the chef -- E. Michael Reidt -- combines a passion for Brazil with his experience as a classically-trained French chef. I would have to say that the website is exquisitely done -- great web designer, whoever it was. http://restaurantsevilla.com/ I would have to say the restaurant's interior is exquisitely done -- great interior designer, whoever it was. I would like to the food was exquisitely done -- but I can't. First of all, as you walk in, the very sexy, romantic and well apportioned dining rooms are to your left. It *is* beautiful. To the right is the bar, filled with dark wood, dim lights -- it could be sexy and romantic, except for the pounding techno music that spills into the main dining room as well. And straight ahead of you as you walk in, behind the hostess' podium, is the largest video display of a glass of red wine in front of a roaring fireplace I've ever seen -- think huge plasma flat-panel TV turned on its side (so it's tall and narrow). Why??? The menu inside the restaurant is lacking many of the items of the menus shown online, and while Lynn and I had no specific dishes in mind to order from what we read online, the actual menu featured fewer selections and looked much less interesting. The combinations of ingedients were often very odd, and we thought about leaving before we even ordered. Eventually we both found one appetizer and one entre each that we thought would work. I had the grilled romaine salad with shaved Parmesean, "vaca frita" and a roasted garlic dressing -- one of those architectural plates that one had to destroy in order to eat. it was smokey (I guess that's from the grilled), not at all garlicky, and overall rather bland and simply "odd." Lynn ordered something called a "Green Crunch" or "Green Crisp" -- a salad compose with snow peas, green beans, asperagus and slices of warm fingerling potatoes, in a pommegranite dressing. I've never seen a pommegranite dressng that was white before. It felt like a handful of veggies thrown together -- the snow peas were crisp and tasty, for example, but nothing tied the dish together and ultimately, as a dish (rather than as a plate of individual items), it was tasteless. We also each had a glass of Sancerre. For our entres, Lynn ordered the chicken breast (the menu said it was on a bed of celery root, but it tasted suspiciously like potatoes); as Lynn said, the chicken was good, but nothing special. I had the duck breast & leg (overly salty, overly dry, and overly fatty). We each had a glass of 2004 Bourgogne rouge. We skipped coffee and dessert. The bill was approx. $125 for a very disjointed and disappointing meal. (In fairness, I should probably add that the two women at the next table enjoyed their flat-iron steak, but I'll have to take their word for it -- i won't be going back any time soon.) Jason

All set on the walls with no respectful distance between them, cramped almost as if the viewer is meant to have the works of at least five artistic titans in their field of vision at once and at all times. It is breathtaking! It is a pity that The Barnes became a political issue. I think most of us would have liked to have seen the collection stay just where it is, peaceful and undisturbed silently greeting worshipers from around the globe, content in knowing its effect on those for whom art is the measure of how we distinguish the barbarians from the rest of us. The new Barnes will open on the Parkway. Some will boycott it for a while. And gradually, the collection will have its way. And in ten years or less, the furor will be memory and we the natives, and visitors from around the globe will flock again to this extraordinary assemblage of the works of the Masters. That being said, our service was so terrible at Bindi that it is difficult to even remember the food. Our server, Karen, was inattentive and cold, and seemed annoyed at simple questions we posed about the dishes. When she brought out a dish that I had not ordered, she tried to convince me that I did! When I insisted she sighed audibly and walked away in an evident huff. She didn't swing by the table for the next 15 minutes and I had to ask other employees about where my correct order was. I couldn't believe she would treat customers this way and still expect a tip! And that is when I remembered that she was guaranteed 18% of our check because of the size of our party. text: Ok St Louisans: for some reason Kaldi's has gotten a big name as the premiere local coffee house. It has all the hype, but none of the follow through. In a city full of hipsters that claims to be as anti-Starbucks as any other, I might imagine that there would exist a local craze substitute. But as far as I can tell, Kaldi's is not it. The Good. To be fair, Kaldi's has great service. The baristas are always polite and in a good mood (with the exception of the 5-minute pre-closing drop in, but I would be angry at me too if I stopped in then). The Bad. For some unknown reason, Kaldi's on the weekend is a family hot spot. There is no instrument that has been created to measure how inappropriate it is to have screaming small children running around a coffee house for two main reasons: one, early Saturday morning the last thing I need is anyone screaming before I have at least two cups of coffee; two, and I cannot stress this one enough, coffee is hot (even McDonald's warns us about this now). When small children run around people holding hot, uncovered beverages disaster is not only likely, but absolutely going to ensue. The Ugly. The drip coffee is always burnt. There is just no way to go through it fast enough to not be. The espresso drinks are equal to the quality of any other coffee shop, nothing to write home about, and certainly not better than, god-forbid, Starbucks. The food is fine, but I can crank out a scone as well as Kaldi's. Overall, I have given this chain (yep, I am going to call it that) enough chances. Either I am driving home to use my Mr Coffee for a nice fresh cup, or going up to Delmar. Stop calling this thing a local coffee house, in all my experience it is, at best, a cheap imitation.

Over 15 types of grilled cheese (their specialty), like 10 types of cheese fries... they have some of my friend's favorites - lobster mac and cheese, sliders... and a grease truck sandwich that will either make you drool or vomit. They have ice cream, of course, as well as other dessert items... I like how every time I go, my ice cream choices get complimented. :) Maybe I really am the best orderer in the world. If so, I recommend the warm cookie pie with cookie dough ice cream and hot fudge. They also have specials for each day of the week - weiner wednesdays, sundae sundays... you get the idea. The only day that doesn't have a special is what I've taken to calling, 'F-you Fridays'. Saturdays has some free food if you wear pajamas, but there's fine print I can see on the sign because it's behind the soft serve. If I had one thing I would change about the Pop Shop, it would be this: Baffles The place needs baffles. It's a big open room, with high ceilings and nothing to absorb sound at all. text: I'll admit, I have a tough time with shaving products. Men have to be trained to shave by those they grow up with, and for those of us who weren't taught properly, all I can say is, thank goodness for Art of Shaving! Their process is amazing, and I'm happy to say its all available, relatively inexpensively, through this great King of Prussia store. The store holds everything you'd need for men who need help grooming their non-scalp hair. There's a wide variety of shaving creams in different scents, including lemon, lavender, and sandalwood. Sandalwood is my favorite. There are matching oils for pre-shaving lubrication and aftershaves in the same scents to keep it all in the same family. What's more is that they have a great selection of shaving brushes to make lathering more effective. All of these products may give you sticker shock when you first walk in. $20-some for shaving cream?! Okay, but it comes in a big tub, and it's not the GEL kind, so you only need a VERY little dab of it on your shaving brush, and it lasts for months, so it's even cheaper than something from CVS. $100 for a nice shaving brush? Okay, but, they last for 10 years, so that's really $10 a year to give you a far closer shave. The store is set up with wonderful displays on dark mahogany shelves which gives you a classic and manly feel. There are big starter kits for around $100 which includes the oil, a large shaving cream, aftershave, and the lowest-end shaving brush, which makes a great gift set. There's a small, travel size kit, which may be more ideal. The body products, though I've used a few, are heavily scented so be warned. I mainly go there to replenish their awesome shaving cream, but they also have personal barber services, so be sure to ask the salespeople when they'll be in. All the staff has been VERY friendly, and always gives me tons of free samples and explains new products. Honestly, some of the best shopping experiences I've ever had in the King of Prussia Mall.

The entrees were slow roasted pork loin, parmesan dusted chicken cutlets and the seared tuna special. The pork was done in a fairly appalling cinnamon overloaded apple filling way, which was an insult to any self-respecting pig! The meat was also dry and had no "slow roasted" appeal at all. The tuna was the worst: A very thin slice of tuna weakly overcooked on one side and medium on the other...not "seared" at all (which in my opinion should be a thick piece very shortly cooked at high temp on both sides...go to the close-by "Fresca" at The Pier and have their seared tuna salad if you like it nicely done)! It came with a few stalks of asparagus which were practically raw...a sad showing! The service was acceptable, even thought the waitresses had the plastic charm of inflated barbie dolls. Bottom line: Do not go there for dinner...maybe have the bruschetta for lunch some day. If you like italian, go to the Cafe Amaretto...considerably cheaper and much more authentic.

The pasta has been terrible the 2 times I've tried it - seriously overcooked noodles with bland sauces laid on top. I do enjoy the antipasti and the simple salads are acceptable. In the past we went with family groups on Sunday nights primarily for the 2-1 beer and the location. Mafiaoza's has been looking shabby recently as well. I'd be very happy with a new restaurant on 12th South.

Just as the baby was falling asleep (about 11:30) the front desk called to say we should have checked out already. Now, with only about an hour left and any hopes of a nap for our little guy - i settled him down, and wouldn't you know it, another employee pounds on our door (he had towels; we didn't ask for towels!) --- OH! and I should mention - we put the "NOT NOW" sign IN the door lock yet they still disturbed us. The hotel is cute, but not being afforded the opportunity to rest peacefully has left us extremely disappointed in this hotel. text: There is nothing in Tampa that deserves 5 stars. That being said, there are only a few restaurants in the whole of the US that dry age their prime steak as long as Bern's does. While the campy decor and sometimes uneven service may relegate Bern's to the almost great, it is an original Tampa treasure, far exceeding any of the chain steakhouses it competes against.

My personal favorite is the Brad's Beef which was a great sandwich comprised of roast beef, provolone cheese, green chiles, red onions and dressing. I'm definitely not a fan of veggies in my food but the chiles actually go very well to complement the beef. The bread part of my sandwich was certainly good but it was not "beyond" as advertised. The service here is always fairly quick and the workers have always eagerly awaited my order with smiles. text: Let me start by saying that we live in the neighborhood and that this was our favorite go-to bar for years. We would come here with friends from out-of-town, after a really late night at work for dinner, and sometimes on a random afternoon for a cold drink on a hot and sweaty day when we were too gross to go anywhere else. We had made this place part of our lives. My father-in-law had been here back in the 80's and was thrilled to see new ownership. My best friend (raised by a bar-owning family) had given it approval way before the Philly Weekly did. Reasons we loved it back then: blackened green beans, fries like at Monk's when you don't want to deal with the wait there, great beer selection, unpretentious, perfect amount of dive and grime. But we had a inconceivable experience about a year and a half ago and have never been back. And I think that other people should skip it as well. January 1, 2009. I know it was a holiday and bad manners can sometimes be excused by the stress that comes with it, but bear with me. My cousins and brother are in-town and we are headed to the Poconos the next day for our annual, under-40, family ski-day. We drop by Grace's for a low-key dinner and some beers. It's not that crowded and we get the big round table without much wait. My cousin, who has learning disabilities and is also a bartender, goes to order a beer he had never heard of before and has trouble pronouncing it (I know you have all had this problem with imports somewhere). He tries to order the beer and the bartender snaps at him because he can't understand what he said. My cousin becomes flustered and apologizes and says he didn't know how to pronounce it. The bartender snarls, "If your mouth wasn't full when you were trying to talk, I could hear what you were saying." My cousin wasn't eating. My cousin then proceeds to says that he is sorry, he has dyslexia, points to the menu, and asks how to pronounce it. The bartender essentially calls him a liar. At this point in time, I talk my slightly inebriated kid brother out of starting a honor fight on his cousin's behalf and we (now unhappily) finish our dinner and our round and go to leave. I've had conversations with this bartender before. He's given me samples, offered beer education, mentioned his favorite books. I figure he is having an off-night. On the way out, I approach the bartender and tell him about how we are regulars, about how my cousin does have disabilities, and that I am upset by how he treated my family. He essentially tells me to go fuck myself. Again, I have to talk my kid brother out of a brawl. And that is why I have given up blackened green beans.
label: NEG

You've got your Swan Lake fingering, your Manos, your Cascade 220 - something for every taste and budget. Oh how I love their lush selection of Manos in all its myriad colors. I love that I can still get plenty of Rowan and Koigu here, too. Yes, the shop is still tiny, but that's part of the charm and I take my yarn home to wind rather that risk whacking someone with the swift. Rosie's is one of those neighborhood places where you have to go a few times to sort of feel like you belong. I like the staff and have never had a problem. If you're feeling neglected, speak up! If I'm new to a particular shop, I sometimes feel awkward and out of place. text: After a trip to Hong Kong Market and then finding out that Pho Tau Bay was closed, I noticed Tan Dinh on the drive and made a highly illegal several turns to make it to the entrance. My friend and I walk in and the first thing I noticed, to be honest, was that there were no Vietnamese people in sight. The interior is large and bright, well-decorated, and... it doesn't smell like anything. It doesn't have that Vietnamese restaurant smell, of MSG and days-brewed stock. Hm, I think to myself. Okay. Tan Dinh has a huge menu, phone-book status, and when in doubt, I usually fall back to my staple Pho Tai Gau (rare steak and brisket). My friend got her pho with tendon, and we shared an order of Cha Gio (eggrolls). Pho - Very Americanized. The broth was too sweet and the portion size was ENORMOUS. However... a lot of mediocrity... is still mediocre. I tried balancing the broth with Sriracha, which didn't really work at all. It did come with a lot of veggies, however, including cilantro and mint, with the usual basil, sprouts, and lime. I actually couldn't force myself to finish the entire bowl. Cha Gio - Bubbly crispy rice paper, rather than the wheat-based eggroll wrapping paper, was a plus! Minus... the eggrolls were too large and weren't cut in half. They were full of a mediocre filling of some sort of pork byproduct; barely any shrimp or vegetables to round it out. Bland, bland, bland. The nuoc mam (fish sauce) came in a bottle at the table (weird, right?) and was also too sweet. Later on in the day, some Vietnamese people came in and, since I'm creepy, I noticed that none of their tables actually ordered the pho. One table had squab that looked delicious. I'm willing to give this place another shot and update my review at another time.
label: NEG

text: I don't understand the high amount of positive reviews for Sushi Brothers. In a city with a glaring lack of quality sushi restaurants, maybe people are more forgiving in their critiques. The problem is that Sushi Brothers is just not very good even when compared to the other places in town. THE GOOD Yellowtail Roll: Pretty much the only thing I completely enjoyed. I like their combo of yellowtail, smelt roe, and avocado as opposed to the more traditional green onion that typically goes with yellowtail. Fortunately this particular cut of fish tasted fresh. THE BAD Crawfish Roll: They drench their crawfish in spicy mayo sauce. I HATE rolls drenched in sauce. You couldn't even taste the crawfish. Gross. Why do people insist on over-saucing sushi??? Don't you want to be able to taste what you're actually eating? Squid Steak: Over-cooked squid, soaked in butter. I know that it's traditionally prepared with butter but I've had squid steak many times at other sushi places and the aroma/flavor of butter has never overwhelmed the squid like it did here. Bad, bad news. Assorted Veggie Tempura: I originally thought these were decent, but upon reflection I realize that was probably just the hunger talking. Wayyyyy too overbattered, not crunchy at all, made it very tough to eat. I would not recommend ordering tempura in any form from them if that's how they batter their food. House Special Roll: They double-wrapped the seaweed around the roll, making it hard to chew through. Come on guys. Even if I can get through it, that's unacceptable. PURGATORY Levee Voice Roll: One of their "Special New Rolls" that has potential as it was something I'd never seen in a roll before. They placed a Blue Crab "paste" on the top of the roll that would have been quite delicious if they didn't smother it with sauce. And of course the nasty crawfish was inside too. If I had to go to Sushi Brothers again, I would order this roll but ask for no sauce and subbing out the crawfish for something else. Service: It wasn't bad in terms of neglect, but everyone there was so awkward that it made me pseudo-uncomfortable. And it had nothing to do with a language barrier too, as all the servers and bussers were ABCs (or ABVs most probably). Hard to describe. Just weird. Fortunately they're pretty good about requests, as they allowed us to get the rolls cut into 8 pieces and also sub out soy paper for regular seaweed (seriously, why does anyone like soy paper? It tastes literally like a piece of paper in your mouth). OVERALL Can't quite give it 1-star because at the very least I would come here again for the Levee Voice Roll (modified) if someone else really wanted to, but it definitely would not be recommended. There are better places, even in a sushi-starved city like New Orleans.
label: NEG

text: For our inaugural trek to Reno on what could only be described as a weekend of pure romance, my husband and I chose the Silver Legacy. Hey, it's good enough for the Go-Gos and Engelbert Humperdink. Let's be honest here, it's definitely not the Four Seasons but (maybe because our expectations were low) we were very pleasantly surprised by our experience there. These people know how to keep you entertained.....at a low price point. Once the burning sensation in my nose subsided (I attribute it to maxed out A/C and in-door smoking), I started to recognize this place for what it was. A superbly run land-based cruise ship...the kind with all-night gambling. The demographic was as expected and then some. We had the senior contingency, the rockers in their concert tees (I had a weird compulsion to rat my bangs) and the bizarro-land, cougar-esque singles scene (the place has 2 nightclub/lounges and 2 or 3 other bars. But what I didn't expect was the huge number of families. There were strollers galore...Reno ain't just for your uncle's cousin's girlfriend's aunt anymore. Maybe it's because the El Dorado, the Silver Legacy and Circus Circus are all connected via this indoor walkway that channels some bizarro-land underground city - we literally didn't go outside until we left on Sunday - but I love this place for all that it is: $5 blackjack tables all night, great service, cheap eats and some damn good people watching. It doesn't hurt that they cater to the Asians -- I had hot & sour soup one night and it was pretty damn good. Did you know that the Silver Legacy has a Head of Asian Games? Is that the best title ever? We left up over $200. Anywhere else that would be nothing, but in Reno it paid for most of our trip. Needless to say, I'll be back.. In summary, cheap food + cheap tables + clean + good service + ample amenities = a worthwhile visit to the Biggest Little City.

text: Switching hair salons is always a terrifying experience. I recently had to find a new hair salon because my girl had a baby and decided to retire (The audacity, I know!) My sister had been telling me for months to go to Clare. I just let my roots grow to my ears and my hair split well, more or less to my ears. Finally, I relented when one day I finally gave my hair a good long look in the mirror and realized, I was in trouble. This, seriously, might be the best my hair has ever looked. Keep in mind, I do not have easy hair to deal with. My hair is incredibly curly, and not in that pretty Keri Russell kind of way, in that bad, Julia Roberts in My Best Friend's Wedding kind of way. Whatever Clare did to me, it worked. My hair is shiny, my curls are bouncy and not frizzy at all, and it straightens out with little to no struggle from me and my round brush. Also my high lights...I can't brag enough about my high lights! It has never looked so real. If you put my hair next to that of my 19 month old niece, you couldn't tell the difference. It's amazing! In terms of personality, Clare is the nicest, funniest person to speak to as well. It was a completely pleasant experience having my hair done. She even squeezed me in at the end of her day knowing I was in desperate shape. Also, the price was a lot cheaper than a lot of places around Clayton. For a whole head of high lights and a massive clean up on my hair, it only cost me $140 bucks and that included tip! If you are looking for a new hair salon, go here. The only draw back is finding parking in Clayton. But that's always miserable.

text: 5 Stars for the half brother of "The Birchrunville Cafe" If it's possible for there to be a more quaint location for a restaurant than Birchrunville Pa, its St. Peter's VIllage. The restaurant resides in an Inn, tucked far in the woods of Chester County. You'll cross many steel bridges, on roads so narrow, were you to come across another car, you would have to back up for miles at a time. ok maybe I'm embellishing just a tad, but the drive is half of the adventure. The dining room is very formal with heavy gold and crimson striped window treatments, thick starched tablecloths and a slight aroma of septuagenarians. Thankfully the staff softens the decor with friendly, attentive service. The menu will feel familiar to those acquainted with the Birchrunville. The big difference here is the wine list. For PA, they did a great job. Last time I was there my table enjoyed a bottle of Kreydenwiess Pinot Blanc "Kritt". Of course the wine was mis-labeled on the list, but at least they had it!!! The food is great, but it's the beauty of the pristine and rustic landscape that makes The Inn at St. Peters special. Oh, and make sure to take your coffee to the outdoor deck so that you can appreciate the babbling creek lush forest and wildlife while you digest a little piece of perfection If you go, you'll never forget it.

text: Call me the Grinch or rather "The childless Grinch who abhors mass commercialism that occurs at a rampant pace during the holidays." Linvilla is a torrent of Xmas commercialism gone bad. Perhaps I would be singing a different tune if I had kids and brought them here for Halloween and the holidays to do what kids do at these things - like pet animals, or eat caramel apples, go on a hayride or go and cut down the Griswold family Xmas tree. But I don't, so bah-humbug. Don't get me wrong, I love the holidays - the whole bit - trimming the tree, snow, carols, the whole nine yards - I just hate how commercialized it can all get and quick - and Linvilla is feeding into that holiday frenzy, appealing to the kiddies, and getting a mad pay-off for it. Huge parking area, a bevy of stores with all sorts of trinkets, and tzotchkes, with, almost as an afterthought, some greenery, some sad looking pre-cut trees (at $50- $90 a pop- why not just buy a tree in the city?) and the "go and cut down your own tree' experience (for $60, and you must get on a hayride - which isn't really - to get there and back - the whole thing can take an hour and a half at the very least)- which really isn't as fun or idyllic as it sounds. I was anticipating the kiddies, yes, I suppose, but I wasn't anticipating that I'd feel like I was shopping at a mall when I decided to go to a place whose name includes "orchards" in it. There was nothing outdoors-y, intimate or Christmas-esque about the experience or the place at all, save the fact, that it was indeed, located in the outdoors. It was crowded, kind of a mad-house and I felt like I was being price-gouged left and right. After assessing the whole scene, I understood that it was to be expected - it's not like Linvilla is out in the country, it's smack dab in between suburbs, and thus resulting in creating Suburban Orchards with a suburban shopping mall feel. Don't come here for the atmosphere, or to get you in the holiday spirit. It's probably good for kids, but in the only way it can be good for kids, like Disney. Xmas trees here are no better nor cheaper than where you would find them elsewhere.

text: Trophy Bikes is my favorite bike store in Philly, its suburbs, or Manhattan (where I work), and I've shopped at at least a dozen over the past decade. I have bought 2 folding bikes from them, and got a competitive price and accurate, useful information during our bike search for both of the bikes. They gave us plenty of attention, which was especially useful for my wife, who is small and fits very few bikes. Most other shops were not nearly as helpful, didn't have as broad a selection, and seemed willing to sell my wife a bike that was not a good fit for her size and needs. Trophy Bikes is especially good if: 1. You need to buy a good or great folding bike - they are the local experts and have even hosted several regional events to promote folders 2. Need to buy a sturdy, same, fast, stylish, or comfortable urban bike - they know the needs of urban riders, especially commuters 3. Need a simple or difficult repair (their mechanic somehow extracted the broken end of the shift indicator chain end from deep inside my 5 speed sturmey archer hub - you won't find that repair in any manual!), or some advice about fixing your own bike, or spare parts (they have helped me find difficult-to-find parts for my own repairs, and deal with Dahon, who are not very good about stocking older parts or getting parts to consumers). Their new commuter hours (open 8 AM M-F) are great for working people who depend on their bikes. You can also buy some fine sports and touring bikes here, but other shops in the area are also good for these. I've seen some bad comments on yelp about their attitude, but in my experience they have a great attitude and will tell you what they know and what they think, honestly. I'm a nice guy, and I never find them rude. When they are busy, they may not have enough time for you, but they are busy because they are good. And I've had plenty of short treatment and so-so advice from some other shops in Philly that are less busy, but only seem to cater to expensive sports/racing bikes and comfort/hybrid bikes. Also, I've called Trophy at 2 minutes to closing time, and they were willing to stay open 15 minutes late so that I could pick up some parts. While I was finishing my transaction, a guy came even later needing a broken chain fix and Mike set him up and showed him how to fix his chain (the bike was locked up 10 blocks away). The owner, Mike M, is a straight shooter who has also put in a lot of volunteer time on bike advocacy to help make this a safer and more convenient city for bikers (and pedestrians). The only weakness that I find is that they aren't always good with paperwork, but then again neither am I, and they are good with followup and apologetic if they lose something. So I recommend Trophy to urban bikers and commuters, and suggest that if you are thinking about commuting by bike, you make an appointment and spend an hour talking to them and trying some folding bikes. If you buy a good folding bike that fits in your home and workplace, you can stop buying that monthly SEPTA pass or parking permit because you can ride 3 or 4 days a week. You'll be in better physical shape within a month, you'll have paid for your bike within a year, and you'll get in the habit of giving less of your money to oil companies, terrorists, and other dubious characters. What could be better?

text: My husband and I have been to Moe's twice- and both times we enjoyed delicious food and left with full bellies. As it should be, Moe's is a Simpson's themed restaurant (it's in Springfield, after all) but it's not overbearing. Only a few of the dishes (The Flaming Moe- a little confusing- it's a burger- why isn't this on the drink menu?) are named after Simpsons history. We both ordered French Onion soups- not sure why our waitress didn't come out of the kitchen telling us, "Hot stuff coming through" because the stuff was so hot that I burnt my mouth- it still hurts...I digress....but it was good. Not an abundance of cheese but that allowed me to fully enjoy the half rack of ribs that came next...and they were perrrrrrfect. The falling-off-the-bone ratio was equally proportionate to the amount (and smoky tartness) of savory barbecue sauce. Husband enjoyed the Flaming Moe burger- and as he usually does, he ordered it because it was called the flaming Moe, not because he's partial to chipotle. The burgers are good sized and decently priced at $7.99. Todd smartly opted for the $2 upgrade to onion rings since my plate came with fries, it was a win-win. Normally the burgers are paired with Moe's homemade potato chips but pass up O-rings? Pffft. The chipotle sauce that is paired with the burger is where the flaming comes in- I dipped my fries in it and HOLY MOE! It was spicy. Although this time we didn't have the Duff beer since I'm with child, we've had it in the past and it's ice cold and delicious. Most likely, it's a well known light beer but the ice cold part was killer. The bar is a separate part of the same building- that side is the smoking section but it's COMPLETELY closed off so if smoking isn't your thing- no worries about dealing with the second hand air. In all, Moe's is good- it's like any other middle of the road family food joint except the food was hot and appropriately delicious. We were drawn back there because restaurant.com had $25 gift certs for $2 this week- (code is SANTA at checkout- and it's good until the 25th nationwide) the only catch is that you had to spend $40. Food: Small plate special: Arugula salad with grilled red onions, spicy pecans, satsuma pieces, satsuma vinaigrette, topped with grilled duck tenders - The leaves of arugula were huge and chopped! with an astringent flavor much more reminiscent to kale or chard than the usual baby arugula we're used to in restaurant salads. The duck was tender with a slight charred edge at the lean bits of skin. The real hit, though, was the smoky, spicy toasted pecans, which really connected the sweet and tart satsuma with the vegetal arugula and the savory duck. Smoked wagyu beef brisket with garlic parmesan fries - I don't eat brisket often, but when I saw wagyu in the menu description I expected that the fat marbleing would help keep the brisket moist, as with the Joint's barbecue brisket. Sadly this was not the case. The brisket was simply too dry, while the sauce was too thick and did a poor job of acting a wetting agent. The fries were handcut and crisp, there was far too much shaved parmesan and no taste of garlic at all. Applewood smoked scallops with garlicky broccoli, XO sauce, & Sesame Seed Tuille - I'm not sure which of the accoutrement was the sauce that topped the scallops; whichever it was, it was completely delicious. The broccoli was finished by roasting and so was slightly crisp, while the standout was the moist and delicate scallops, perfectly cooked bivalves that had some chew without being tough. Their natural sweetness was brought to the forefront by the various accompanying sauces. Let it be noted that we ordered drinks when we first sat down. We ordered our food, received our appetizer, finished it, and waited for our food without any acknowledgment from our server except when she took our salad plate, at which time she did notice my empty drink glass and asked if I wanted anything further. I asked to see the drink menu, but perhaps wasn't clear enough; when she brought me the cocktails menu and turned away quickly, I wasn't quick enough to ask for a wine menu. We waited for her to return, so I could ask for the wine list; yet could not catch her attention while she was stopping at the other 2 tables. All this time she was talking to the other tables about their food and drink choices, while barely asking us how things were when she dropped off our dishes. After giving us our entrees, when I was finally able to ask her for a wine list, I waited so I could enjoy my beef with a glass of wine. By the time she returned & I could order, Daniel had finished his dinner and was just waiting for me. We didn't even bother looking at the dessert menu. For food, ambience, and price, I would otherwise have given this a 3.5 stars rounded up to 4 (a half star deducted because of the crowdedness and difficulty to get a table). Due to the service we received, I deducted a full star and then rounded down. Yes, we are young, and yes we are Asian. And yes, I believe this is the reason for our treatment. I've never felt so blatantly discriminated against in a restaurant. I really want to like Boucherie and give them a higher rating but I am absolutely appalled at the service we received. There are better restaurants that appreciate our patronage.

text: After all of the glowing reviews here on Yelp, I thought Lacroix would be the perfect place to enjoy some Philadelphia French gastronomy. And while my dining experience had a few hits, unfortunately, the misses will stand out most prominently. First, the hits. The service is great. The waitstaff perfectly balance the high-brow service you expect in a place like this with a smiling, down-to-earth helpfulness that makes you feel welcome. The service is graceful and efficient and encourages you to savor each bite. I began with a dinner salad with a "chocolate" dressing. Which, although it sounded gimmicky, was very good. The only trace of chocolate taste was kind of a darker flavor that complemented the bitterness of the frisee salad beautifully. For an entree, I had the Muscovy Duck Breast which was spectacular. The skin was beautifully browned and crisp, the inside was juicy and flavorful, and the parsnip coconut sauce was creative combination of old and new world flavors that was smooth and rich. Unfortunately, though, there were misses. And they were big ones. My companion had the butter lettuce salad to start, which offered an Asian twist on the traditional butter lettuce salad. And the flavors just didn't work. The chef put sesame oil in the dressing to Asian-it-up a bit, and the pungent flavor of the sesame oil melded with the stinky flavor of the gorgonzola cheese and resulted in completely palate-offending combination. My companion also ordered a side dish of enoki mushrooms with chili sauce which was not only palate-offending, but pretty much inedible. The enokis were soggy and wet (after all they're enoki mushrooms--that's why the Japanese use them in soup) and no amount of thai chili flavor could redeem their sorry state of affairs. And finally our dessert, 5 phases of pumpkin, was disappointing. In the chef's quest for uniqueness and creativity, he forgot that pumpkin is comfort food. And unforch, there was nothing comforting about the 5 measly pieces of odd-flavored pumpkin-oriented minutiae that dotted the dessert plate. Ultimately, the food here tells me that the chef here is very impressed with himself. I also think that if he read this review, he would disdainfully proclaim that "she knows no-ting about zee French cuisine". However, I am too classy to name drop my French gastronomy street cred here. So suffice it to say "zat was zee last time zat I will dine at Lacroix."
